text.text: The agency's media desk in one place: clients, the news moments you are pitching, a contact book of journalists, every pitch with its follow-up date and the coverage it earned. Open the Dashboard on Monday, work pitches that need a follow-up, and log each piece of coverage the day it runs.
The organizations the agency represents, with retainer and ownership.
Each news moment the agency pitches, from planning to wrap-up.
Journalists, editors and producers the agency pitches.
Each pitch sent to a journalist for a campaign, with its follow-up date.
Every earned mention, with outlet, reach and tone.

This workspace runs the media relations side of a PR agency: each client's retainer, goals, spokespeople and key messages, every campaign and its news hook, the media list with how each journalist likes to be pitched, every pitch and follow-up, and the coverage you earn. Monitoring tools and email stay where they are; this is the agency's memory.

pages.title: Writing a pitch that gets read

text.text: Journalists get hundreds of pitches a week and read the first two lines of most. A good pitch is short, specific and written for that one person.
The news hook is real: new, local, surprising, or backed by data
You have read the journalist's last five stories
The spokesperson is approved and free this week
Embargo date agreed with the client, if any

cells.text: The story in under ten words, no hype
Interview, data, photos or an exclusive

text.text: Keep it under 150 words. Paste the press release below your signature, not as an attachment.
Mention a recent story of theirs and why this one fits.
field to note the angle you used, so you can see which ones work.
How they like to be pitched
Offering one outlet the story first can land a bigger piece. Tick
, give them a firm deadline to answer, and do not pitch anyone else until they decide.
One follow-up after two or three working days, with something new: a data point, a photo, a time slot.
A second only if the news is time-sensitive.
Never more than two. Record each in
"Revolutionary", "game-changing", "world-leading" and "excited to announce". They make a story sound like an advertisement.

The Larkspur study pitch to Venture Ledger leads with one number from the survey: how many store managers lost sales to stockouts last quarter. It offers the head of data for a call and the full results under embargo.
Answer within the hour. A journalist who replied is on deadline; a slow answer often loses the story.
A media list goes stale fast: journalists change beats, outlets close, and people move. A clean list means fewer bounced emails, fewer annoyed reporters and better coverage.
How they like to be pitched
Contacts not contacted in 90 days checked: still on the beat, still at the outlet?
Bounced emails fixed or the contact removed
Anyone who asked not to be pitched marked and left alone

text.text: Never add someone to a mass email list. Every pitch is sent by a person to a person.
Never pitch the same story to two reporters at the same outlet without telling them.
Respect embargoes and exclusives exactly as agreed.
If a journalist asks you to stop, stop.
shows how often you contact someone;
shows how often it worked. A contact pitched often with no stories needs better-fitted pitches, or a rest.

Gideon Okafor has not been contacted in three months and his notes say he left the beat. The account executive checks his recent stories, finds he now covers transport, and updates his beat instead of deleting him.
The list belongs to the agency, not to one account executive. Notes from every pitch go on the contact so the next person knows the history.
Clients pay for results they can see. A clear coverage report shows what ran, where, and whether the story said what the client wanted it to say.
Every story gets a row the day it runs:
: national, trade, local, broadcast or podcast
Reach from the outlet's audience figures, with the source noted
Link the story to the client and the campaign.

Campaigns planned and the stories you are chasing

text.text: Not all coverage is equal. One trade story read by the client's buyers can matter more than five local mentions. Lead with impact, then volume.
Log it like any other story, with sentiment Negative. Explain what happened and what you did: a correction requested, a statement given, or a plan to respond. Never leave it out of the report.
Reach is an estimate of audience, not readers of the story. Use it to compare, not to impress. Avoid advertising-value figures; most clients and journalists no longer trust them.

Westbrook's flu clinic campaign earned two local stories. One said queues remained long, so it is logged as negative with the key message missing. The report explains it and proposes a follow-up story on the extra Saturday hours.
Save a copy of every story the day it runs. Links break and paywalls go up, and clients want the clip months later for their own website and sales decks.
Walk through the report in 20 minutes. Ask which story mattered most to the client's business; their answer tells you what to chase next month.
On the day news breaks, everything happens at once. A written runbook means nobody is guessing who sends what, and the client hears the results as they land.

text.text: Stick to the key messages; never guess at numbers.
If a journalist asks something the spokesperson cannot answer, promise a reply by a set time and keep the promise.
Off-the-record means nothing unless the journalist agreed to it first.

If a story breaks before the embargo, call the client first, then release to everyone at once. Do not blame the outlet in public; note it on the contact and decide later whether to trust them with embargoes again.
Log every story with tier, reach and sentiment.
Thank each journalist who covered it.
Pitch follow-up angles to those who did not, with any new data from the launch.
